title: Supe Valley: public buildings and the work of feeding people
question: How can buildings and food traces tell different parts of a community’s history?

summary.title: Coast and valley
summary.text: Caral’s platforms and circular courts place collective building beside a less visible history of food production. Coastal Áspero offers a second setting in the Supe Valley. Comparing them connects monumental spaces with the plants people used, without assuming that every household had the same diet or role.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: platforms and recessed circular courts

sections.title: Provisioning leaves several kinds of evidence
sections.text: The dental-calculus study recovered plant starches from nine people at Áspero and one at Caral. These traces bring food use into an account otherwise dominated by large buildings. The authors consider exchange as one possible explanation for access to some plants. Starch presence is not a measure of the calories supplied by a crop.

citations.locator: Abstract; Discussion: exchange and limits of starch ubiquity

sections.title: Buildings accumulated over time
sections.text: Caral’s urban plan and ceremonial architecture developed over centuries within the broad 3000–1800 BCE frame. A visitor’s view gathers different building episodes. The arrangement supports questions about organized work, but cannot by itself tell us who assigned tasks, whether people volunteered, or how work varied between households.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis, criterion (ii), Integrity and Authenticity

perspectives: Builders and food producers left material traces, not a complete set of personal accounts. A small sample of human remains cannot speak for all valley residents.
scope: A coastal–inland comparison within the Supe Valley, not an account of every American community. Burial samples and building phases have their own dates within the wider site frame.

activity.prompt: Use the account above to choose evidence for two questions: what plants some people consumed, and how public gathering spaces were arranged. What could neither source tell you?
activity.response: Starches address plant use; platforms and courts address spatial arrangement. Neither supplies every household’s diet or a named worker’s explanation of their obligations. Explain the mismatch rather than treating the two sources as interchangeable.

snapshots.text: Around 2400 BCE lies within Caral’s broadly dated development. Platforms and circular gathering spaces orient us to the Supe Valley’s built landscape. They do not establish the same layout or activity in every year; the linked coastal food study has separately dated burial contexts.

title: Nile communities: building, supply and different centres of power
question: What had to happen around a monument to keep people working?

summary.title: Giza, Saqqara and Kerma
summary.text: Royal monuments depended on food, tools, storage and skilled labor. Giza’s excavated settlement exposes some of that supporting work; Saqqara’s chapel wall presents elite commemoration. Farther south, Kerma developed as a distinct Nubian centre. These places belong to connected Nile histories, not one undifferentiated Egyptian society.

citations.locator: Fourth Dynasty settlement and support staff

sections.title: Supply was part of construction
sections.text: AERA identifies bakeries, kitchens, workshops and storage at Giza. Grain held in royal silos could be distributed for bread and beer; raw materials also arrived for tools and furnishings. This explains a chain of provisioning behind construction. It does not identify every worker’s legal status or make one crew representative of all labor in Egypt.

citations.locator: Settlement account: support staff, materials and grain silos

sections.title: Changing places, separate dates
sections.text: The selected Saqqara wall dates to about 2465–2389 BCE, later than much Fourth Dynasty pyramid building. Kerma’s project dates its city’s foundation around 2500 BCE, while warning that continuity from the earlier Pre-Kerma settlement is unproved. Neither the wall nor a later Kerma beaker dates the beginning of an entire society.

citations.locator: City of Kerma: foundation and uncertain continuity

perspectives: Excavated work spaces and an elite tomb image answer different questions. The surviving records do not give equal access to administrators, cooks, craftspeople and their families.
scope: Selected Egyptian and Nubian settings in the later third millennium BCE. Kerma’s later urban layout and the beaker’s second-millennium date are not projected back to 2400 BCE.

activity.prompt: Explain one link between grain storage and monument building. Then name a question about the workers that a grain silo cannot settle.
activity.response: Storage could support regular food preparation for a workforce. That material connection does not reveal a particular worker’s motives, freedom, household circumstances or membership in a named crew.

snapshots.text: Around 2400 BCE falls within the selected Saqqara wall’s museum date range and after Kerma’s approximate foundation. The chapel is evidence of elite funerary representation; Kerma offers a distinct Nubian urban history. The later beaker is a next reading, not an object from this same moment.

citations.locator: City of Kerma: c2500 BCE foundation

title: Orkney: homes, gathering places and a landscape beyond one village
question: Why does the end of a settlement not end the history of its landscape?

summary.title: More than the standing houses
summary.text: Skara Brae’s stone rooms and connected passages reveal domestic arrangements. Maeshowe, the Stones of Stenness and the Ring of Brodgar provide different kinds of built spaces in Orkney. Reading homes alongside burial and ceremonial monuments expands the inquiry beyond one village, while keeping each site’s chronology separate.

sections.title: Construction connects household and communal work
sections.text: The village’s fitted stone furnishings organize cooking, storage and sleeping within compact rooms. Larger tombs and stone circles required different construction tasks. Comparing these remains helps us distinguish domestic from communal settings; the surviving stones do not recover every ceremony or the identity of those who directed the work.

sections.title: A later landscape is not a longer village occupation
sections.text: UNESCO describes an Orkney cultural-landscape tradition around 3000–2000 BCE. That broader range continues after the selected Skara Brae occupation. Some standing stones were re-erected in modern times. Today’s view therefore combines prehistoric construction, losses and conservation rather than presenting one unchanged Neolithic moment.

perspectives: Architecture reveals possible activities more readily than people’s names or beliefs. A ceremonial interpretation is not a recovered script for the event.
scope: Orkney is a justified local focus: unusually varied surviving domestic and monumental evidence makes comparison possible. It does not represent every European farming community.

activity.prompt: Separate three statements: a stone bed survives; people probably slept there; we know who slept there. Which is observation, which is interpretation, and which needs evidence not supplied?
activity.response: The bed’s form is material evidence; sleeping is a functional interpretation. A named occupant needs further evidence. Apply the same distinction when interpreting a stone circle.

snapshots.text: The 2400 BCE view uses Orkney’s broader 3000–2000 BCE monumental-landscape frame. It does not extend Skara Brae’s village occupation to this date. Read the earlier houses alongside burial and ceremonial monuments, whose individual construction histories remain separate.

citations.locator: Printed p17: modeled village ending 2545–2440 cal BCE

title: Southern Mesopotamia: institutions, work and durable accounts
question: How did counting goods become part of organizing a city?

summary.title: Uruk and its surrounding settlements
summary.text: Uruk grew within a landscape of rivers, farming and neighboring settlements. Large institutions handled goods and workers’ rations. Recording quantities on clay made some transactions durable, leaving an unusually visible administrative history alongside buildings and crafted objects.

sections.title: An account serves a practical task
sections.text: The museum’s writing essay connects early tablets with the recording and distribution of resources. Grain, fish and animals could be counted with signs, while names and actions were harder to interpret. This supports an explanation of record keeping as institutional work; it does not make every tablet a complete narrative of a transaction.

citations.locator: Accounting; signs for rations and interpretive limits

sections.title: Political forms changed while cities continued
sections.text: The Uruk account distinguishes late-fourth-millennium growth from the later Early Dynastic city-states, conventionally about 2900–2350 BCE. It describes rulers seeking imported luxury goods through trade or conquest. A tablet dated about 3100–2900 BCE therefore cannot name the rulers or record all political relations of the 2400 BCE world.

perspectives: Administrative records privilege what institutions counted. They are thinner evidence for unrecorded household labor and for people’s own explanations of their lives.
scope: A local urban–hinterland focus explains accounting through related settlement and institutional evidence. It is not a claim that writing arose once, or that all West and Central Asia followed Uruk’s sequence.

activity.prompt: A tablet counts grain but gives no clear action word. Give one defensible conclusion and one conclusion that would need more evidence.
activity.response: It records a quantity associated with grain. Whether that quantity was received, owed or issued may remain uncertain; a particular worker’s biography is still farther beyond the account.

snapshots.text: Around 2400 BCE sits within the museum’s Early Dynastic city-state frame. Uruk continued after the earlier spread of its material culture. The selected grain tablet is older: use it to investigate accounting practices, not as a direct record of this selected year.

title: Indus settlements: managing water in different places
question: How did water problems shape the work of building a city?

summary.title: Dholavira and Mohenjo-daro
summary.text: Dholavira stood on arid Khadir Island, where seasonal streams and storage mattered. Mohenjo-daro developed beside the Indus, with brick streets, wells and drainage. Their surviving structures let us compare ways of organizing water and inhabited space without assuming identical environments or government.

citations.locator: Description: seasonal streams and water management
Brief synthesis: location, wells and drainage

sections.title: Storage and drainage answer different needs
sections.text: At Dholavira, capturing scarce seasonal water was part of the city’s infrastructure. At Mohenjo-daro, wells and drains formed part of its built layout. Keeping water available and moving unwanted water away are distinct practical tasks. Their remains invite questions about construction and maintenance, but do not identify one ruler who controlled every system.

sections.title: A plan gathers several histories
sections.text: Dholavira’s long occupation and the selected seal’s narrower date range should not be merged. Nor does the regional seal’s collection attribution make it a Dholavira excavation find. Mohenjo-daro’s later Buddhist stupa is a separate addition to the ancient city landscape; it belongs to a different period from the third-millennium urban remains.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: second-century CE Buddhist stupa

perspectives: Buildings and workshop remains expose practical activities. Without a fully deciphered script, they do not supply every resident’s account of authority, rights or maintenance duties.
scope: Two named settlements in different parts of the Indus world. Modern composite plans are not photographs of one simultaneous city layout, and regional object dates are not local construction dates.

activity.prompt: Explain why a reservoir and a drain might both belong in a city. What extra evidence would you need to name the people responsible for maintaining them?
activity.response: Storage retains water for use; drainage carries water away. Their presence supports different infrastructure needs. Administrative records or securely contextualized evidence of labor would be needed to identify particular maintenance arrangements.

snapshots.text: Around 2400 BCE falls within the broad third-millennium Indus urban setting. Compare water management at Dholavira with wells and drainage at Mohenjo-daro. The view marks a regional comparison, not a claim that every visible structure at either site was operating in that exact year.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: third-millennium settlement and urban systems

title: Lower Yangtze: cultivated land, waterworks and unequal burials
question: How do landscapes and objects reveal different kinds of organization?

summary.title: Liangzhu and its surrounding landscape
summary.text: Liangzhu’s city, peripheral waterworks and cemeteries belong to a lower-Yangtze landscape supported by rice cultivation. The city site and Yaoshan burial area offer different evidence: built spaces show organized investment, while differences between graves support interpretations of social distinction.

citations.locator: Description; Brief synthesis: four component areas

sections.title: Infrastructure and social interpretation
sections.text: Water-control works connect cultivated land with the settlement’s surroundings. UNESCO interprets the city layout and differentiated burials as evidence of a regional state. That is an archaeological interpretation of surviving patterns, not a contemporary constitution or a recovered list of everyone’s duties.

sections.title: A jade has its own chronology and limits
sections.text: The selected cong is dated around 2400 BCE. Its wider museum culture label extends beyond the city’s approximately 3300–2300 BCE frame. The catalogue treats the object’s exact function and meaning as uncertain; wealth and status are proposed associations. It cannot identify every belief or the experiences of people outside richly furnished graves.

perspectives: Elaborate objects and differentiated graves make some social distinctions visible. They do not provide equal testimony from farmers, waterworks laborers and those buried with fewer goods.
scope: A justified local focus compares city, waterworks and burial evidence within one documented landscape. Other East Asian settings require their own histories; this is not a universal sequence from farming to statehood.

activity.prompt: Which question is better answered by a dam system, and which by a burial object: how water was managed, or how objects marked distinctions among the dead? Name a limit of each.
activity.response: Dams address water management but do not name every laborer. Burial objects address funerary distinctions but do not reconstruct every living person’s beliefs. Neither alone is a complete social history.

snapshots.text: Around 2400 BCE lies within Liangzhu’s city-site frame and matches the approximate date assigned to the selected jade. Those overlapping dates make comparison possible; they do not establish that this museum object came from the city excavation or that every waterwork was built at this moment.

title: Kuk and An Sơn: reading work in buried landscapes
question: How can ditches, floors and dated deposits reveal different settlement histories?

summary.title: Kuk in the upper Wahgi Valley
summary.text: At Kuk, connected ditches and larger channels redirected water at a wetland margin. Archaeologists interpret this as deliberate preparation for cultivation. This highland setting offers a food-production history whose evidence is different from a city plan, a written account or the later Lapita pottery of island settlements.

citations.locator: Summary of palaeochannels and ditch articulation; drainage for cultivation

sections.title: A mainland comparison with its own sequence
sections.text: At An Sơn in southern Vietnam, the excavators estimate initial occupation around 2500–2200 calibrated BCE. Much of the excavated occupation is later, and the burials later still. Alternating floors and occupation layers suggest houses at ground level, but precise house plans could not be reconstructed. These remains offer a mainland comparison with Kuk; they do not establish migration between the two places.

citations.locator: Introduction: 1997 floors and house interpretation; Chronology: initial and later occupation

sections.title: A network is more than a single cut
sections.text: The investigators describe larger channels receiving water from smaller ditches. Some networks contain right-angled junctions and divisions; others branch differently. Connected cuts make planned drainage a stronger interpretation than an isolated depression would. Shallow cultivation features survive less clearly, so the network does not identify every crop or plot boundary.

citations.locator: Earliest ditch networks; Summary; early network 353

sections.title: Dating a sequence does not fill every year
sections.text: The introduction’s table gives the early Phase 3 range as 4350–3980 calibrated years before 1950, approximately 2400–2030 BCE. Other ditch episodes belong later. The authors lack the precision to date every use of each location. A gap in the dated record cannot simply be filled with an invented uninterrupted sequence.

citations.locator: Subphases: spatial variation and insufficient archaeological precision

perspectives: Earthworks preserve traces of planning and repeated work. They do not name the cultivators or establish their land rights. Modern communities are not represented by archaeological interpretation alone.
scope: Two separate settings: the New Guinea highlands and a southern Vietnamese mound. Their overlapping broad dates are not a route or shared political history. Lapita is a later reading destination, not evidence of a 2400 BCE island migration.

activity.prompt: Explain why linked channels support a drainage interpretation. Then distinguish the approximate date range from a claim that every plot was cultivated every year.
activity.response: Smaller ditches joining larger channels provide a route for water to leave the margin. Dated fills and stratigraphy place episodes in broad ranges; they do not establish continuous annual use of every field.

snapshots.text: Around 2400 BCE is near Kuk’s rounded early Phase 3 boundary and within An Sơn’s estimated initial-occupation range. These are independent archaeological chronologies, not exact events in the selected year. An Sơn’s later houses and burials cannot all be assigned to its beginning. Lapita remains a later comparison.

title: Earthwork communities in different American landscapes
question: Does a large building project tell us how people obtained food or organized work?

summary.title: Supe, the Gulf Coast and the lower Mississippi
summary.text: Caral’s later building history, San Lorenzo’s constructed landscape and Poverty Point’s earthworks belong to different places and sequences. Large public spaces make collective work visible. They do not require us to assume one farming system, one political structure or contact among all three communities.

sections.title: Provisioning does not have one recipe
sections.text: Poverty Point’s hunter-fisher-gatherer communities used varied local foods while obtaining materials from farther away. In the Gulf Coast account, pottery and earth building accompany a different environmental and social history. Monument size alone cannot tell us whether every builder farmed, how food was distributed, or whether all work was compulsory.

citations.locator: San Lorenzo: pottery and monumental landscape

sections.title: A place changes without every community ending
sections.text: Caral’s broad development frame ends before 1200 BCE. Poverty Point’s main complex belongs to about 1700–1100 BCE, while San Lorenzo and later La Venta have separately described peaks. The appearance of a new prominent centre should not be read as the disappearance of all people or craft production at the earlier one.

citations.locator: After about 900 B.C.; later production at other centres

perspectives: Earthmoving and food remains bring builders and provisioners into view, but most individual arrangements of work are unrecovered. Museum labels describe evidence categories, not a single American people.
scope: Three selected settings, not a uniform American sequence. The old Caral record is a comparison across time, not a settlement extended into the 1200 BCE snapshot.

activity.prompt: A visitor says that large earthworks prove every community grew the same crops. Use one food record and one dated site to revise that claim.
activity.response: Use Poverty Point’s hunter-fisher-gatherer food evidence to separate subsistence from monument size. Then identify a particular site and date range; similar earthworks alone do not establish the same food system or contact.

snapshots.text: Around 1200 BCE, Poverty Point and San Lorenzo provide distinct settlement settings. Caral’s retained development range has already ended. Compare the earthworks and evidence of provisioning without placing all three at one simultaneous peak.

title: Kerma and the Nile: goods, institutions and changing control
question: How can exchange and political domination leave different evidence?

summary.title: A Nubian city and its northern neighbours
summary.text: Kerma’s craft production and imported burial goods reveal both local skill and exchange with Egypt. Relations also included conflict and diplomacy. The selected beaker makes ceramic work visible; it cannot stand for every household or for the full history of Nile politics.

sections.title: Making goods and moving goods are different tasks
sections.text: The project identifies institutions, walls and tombs in successive Kerma phases. Imported objects in tombs show the movement and selective use of goods. They do not name every producer, trader or carrier, and elite burial equipment does not measure ordinary household access.

citations.locator: Key Events: imports and local burial equipment

sections.title: The 1200 BCE setting comes after Kerma’s kingdom
sections.text: The museum places Upper Nubia under Egyptian control within a broad 1500–1070 BCE frame. It describes new settlements, temples and administration, including Napata near Jebel Barkal. This later institutional setting must be distinguished from Kerma’s earlier urban kingdom and the still earlier manufacture of the selected beaker.

citations.locator: Upper Nubia timeline; Key Events c1550–1070 BCE

perspectives: Tombs privilege selected elites; temples and administrative labels privilege institutions. Potters and other workers are visible through objects, without a complete record of their own accounts.
scope: Selected Nile and Nubian settings, not all African communities. Differing project and museum Kerma endpoints remain in the linked dossier; no exact universal conquest year is imposed.

activity.prompt: Distinguish what an imported burial object shows from what an administrative chronology shows. Why is the beaker not a 1200 BCE object?
activity.response: An import supports movement and burial use of a good; the chronology describes a broader political arrangement. The beaker has its own earlier catalogue range, so it is a comparison rather than a contemporary object.

snapshots.text: The selected Nile setting around 1200 BCE is Egyptian administration in Nubia, including temple and settlement development. Kerma’s earlier kingdom and the beaker remain earlier readings. Political control did not make every local person, craft or experience identical.

citations.locator: Upper Nubia: c1500–1070 BCE; Key Events c1550–1070 BCE

title: Palaces, workshops and farms across Bronze Age Europe
question: Whose work becomes visible when we look beyond a palace?

summary.title: Crete, mainland Greece and Britain
summary.text: Cretan centres such as Knossos and Phaistos concentrated goods, craft activity and record keeping. Mainland Greek centres provide later workshop and administrative evidence. British farms and fields offer a different settlement pattern within a longer Bronze Age frame.

sections.title: Records make some labour easier to see
sections.text: Clay records and specialized production show how some Aegean institutions organized resources. Britain’s round houses and field divisions instead draw attention to cultivation and household space. Different surviving evidence changes the questions we can answer; a place without palace records is not a place without skilled organization.

sections.title: Change was not synchronized
sections.text: The Cretan destruction horizon around 1450 BCE precedes the late-thirteenth-century destructions described for mainland centres. Britain’s broad Bronze Age sequence continues beyond both. The Uluburun cargo offers a comparison for circulating materials, not a proven route linking each of these selected places.

perspectives: Institutional accounts favour the categories their record keepers needed. Farms and workshops expose other practical tasks, without supplying every worker’s voice or status.
scope: Selected contrasting settings, not one European government or a common collapse. Uluburun is a cross-regional reading destination; no European origin or destination is assigned to its voyage.

activity.prompt: Choose a palace record and a field boundary as evidence. What work might each reveal, and why can neither prove one Europe-wide collapse?
activity.response: A record can identify institutional goods or labour categories; a field boundary can show organization of land. Each needs its own place and date. Neither extends a local destruction horizon to all European communities.

snapshots.text: Around 1200 BCE, the mainland Greek account describes destruction and declining palace institutions. British farming landscapes belong to a different, longer sequence. This comparison shows uneven change; it does not establish one event or cause across Europe.

title: Hattusha and Uluburun: institutions on land and cargo at sea
question: How can a city and a shipwreck reveal different kinds of organization?

summary.title: A capital and a cargo assemblage
summary.text: Hattusha’s palace, temples and archives reveal institutions within an Anatolian capital. The Uluburun wreck preserves a dated cargo off the southern coast of Anatolia. A city’s accumulated buildings and a ship’s lost load are different kinds of evidence, even when they belong within overlapping broad histories.

citations.locator: Project overview: capital and cult centre

sections.title: A cargo is not a complete trade network
sections.text: The wreck’s varied goods support questions about supply, loading and maritime exchange. They do not recover every port visited, the identity of all people aboard or a single merchant’s itinerary. Hattusha’s institutional evidence cannot fill those missing details merely because both places belong in an eastern Mediterranean inquiry.

sections.title: An institutional ending is not every resident’s ending
sections.text: The DAI overview frames Hattusha’s capital history approximately from 1650 to 1180 BCE and also describes later occupation. Composite city plans gather different phases. Around 1200 BCE, the broad capital frame is relevant; a precise citywide destruction date or a single cause cannot be inferred from that range.

perspectives: Palace records favour institutional concerns, while a wreck records a loss. Neither gives an ordinary household census or a full account from the people who moved the goods.
scope: Anatolian and maritime settings, not all West or Central Asia. The disputed drought/collapse causal claim is not used to fill this orientation; cargo origins and routes retain the dossier’s qualifications.

activity.prompt: A cargo contains materials from different regions. What does that support, and what additional evidence would be needed to draw a ship’s route?
activity.response: It supports circulation and assembly of goods. A route needs evidence for particular ports and voyage stages; a material’s origin alone cannot show each intermediate stop or identify the crew.

snapshots.text: Around 1200 BCE lies near the end of Hattusha’s broad capital-era frame. Its buildings represent multiple phases. Uluburun’s earlier cargo provides a separate exchange comparison, not a shipwreck dated to this selected year or proof of one cause of political change.

title: After major Indus cities: different settlement histories
question: How can we follow change without extending an earlier city’s lifespan?

summary.title: Dholavira and Bhagwanpura
summary.text: Dholavira’s changing urban layout belongs to a long occupation ending before this chapter’s 1200 BCE snapshot. Bhagwanpura, in the Kurukshetra district, supplies a separately dated village sequence. Reading the two together shifts attention from a single urban ending to differently situated communities.

sections.title: Pottery changes within an occupied place
sections.text: Kenoyer summarizes Bhagwanpura’s Late Harappan phase as 1700–1300 BCE and its Painted Grey Ware phase as 1400–1000 BCE. Some layers contain both pottery traditions. Their overlap supports investigation of local change and interaction rather than a simple empty interval between two named cultures.

citations.locator: Printed p43: chronology and mixed layers

sections.title: A material label does not identify a language
sections.text: The chapter describes changing pottery and differently shaped houses. It also cautions that pottery cannot determine the inhabitants’ language or religion. Earlier urban water systems at Dholavira remain a useful comparison for practical organization, but they cannot be assigned to Bhagwanpura or carried forward to 1200 BCE.

citations.locator: Printed p43: houses and limits of linguistic/religious identification

perspectives: Settlement remains expose household activities without supplying individual testimony. Archaeological classifications are not direct statements of how inhabitants named themselves.
scope: Two separately dated settings. Bhagwanpura’s dates follow the cited scholarly synthesis of the excavation; the entire excavation report has not been reviewed. Textual epic identification and racial interpretations are not adopted.

activity.prompt: Why can mixed pottery in a layer support a question about interaction without proving that everyone spoke the same language?
activity.response: The layer associates material traditions in a particular context. Speech and religious identity require different evidence. Also retain the possibility that deposit formation affects associations rather than assigning each pot to a distinct ethnic group.

snapshots.text: Around 1200 BCE falls within the cited 1400–1000 BCE Bhagwanpura phase. It is a later village setting, separate from Dholavira’s earlier urban occupation. The phase range does not date every house or pottery change to this exact year.

title: Yin Xu: craft, divination and royal institutions
question: What do royal records reveal, and whose experience do they leave out?

summary.title: A focused late-Shang setting
summary.text: Yin Xu near Anyang contains palace and ancestral-shrine areas, tombs and evidence of specialized craft. Oracle-bone inscriptions preserve particular questions and divinatory practices. These records open a view into royal institutions; they do not represent all communities across East Asia.

sections.title: Objects and inscriptions answer different questions
sections.text: A bronze vessel can expose choices of form, casting and use in ritual settings. An oracle inscription records a different activity: posing and interpreting a divinatory question. The selected museum objects have their own catalogue attributions; neither should be assigned to a particular excavated tomb without provenance evidence.

sections.title: The late capital is not the entire dynasty
sections.text: UNESCO dates Yin Xu’s late-capital frame to about 1300–1046 BCE. The broader Shang convention starts earlier. A change in dynasty around 1046 BCE should therefore be kept apart from transformations around 1200 BCE in distant Anatolia and the Aegean.

perspectives: Royal tombs and divination records favour court priorities. The labour of makers is visible through production, while ordinary residents’ own narratives remain much harder to recover.
scope: A justified local focus: shrine, burial and craft contexts at one late capital let us compare evidence types closely. This does not claim continuous coverage of every East Asian region or dynasty.

activity.prompt: Compare what a vessel’s manufacture and an inscribed question can tell you. Name one thing neither establishes about an ordinary family.
activity.response: Manufacture can reveal materials and skilled production; an inscription can reveal a recorded institutional concern. Neither alone establishes an ordinary family’s diet, political choices or access to those objects.

snapshots.text: Around 1200 BCE lies within Yin Xu’s late-Shang capital frame. Palace, shrine, tomb and divination evidence offer related but distinct views of institutions. The later Shang–Zhou transition is not moved back to this snapshot date.

title: Kuk, An Sơn and Lapita: sequences across land and sea
question: Why must farming, burial and island-settlement evidence keep separate dates?

summary.title: Three independent archaeological settings
summary.text: Kuk’s highland cultivation history, An Sơn’s mainland settlement and burial sequence, and Lapita pottery in island communities preserve different activities. Bringing them together broadens the regional view without making them stages of one migration or one economy.

sections.title: Local deposits record different work
sections.text: Kuk’s ditch networks concern water control. At An Sơn, occupation layers and later burials require separate dating. Pottery in Lapita settings can instead help investigate manufacture and circulation among island communities. Similar broad dates do not demonstrate that people at all three places followed the same farming or settlement practices.

sections.title: Island sequences cannot be backdated as a group
sections.text: The institutional account places Lapita emergence in the Bismarcks around 1500 BCE and a broad movement toward Remote Oceania around 1100–800 BCE. Particular Tongan sites have their own modeled dates. The earlier part of this chapter must not be filled with later Tongan settlement evidence.

perspectives: Archaeological evidence records actions through deposits and objects. It does not recover the identities of every cultivator, potter or voyager, and modern descendant communities are not interchangeable.
scope: Selected highland, mainland and island histories. Overlapping intervals are not an established route linking Kuk, An Sơn and every Lapita settlement.

activity.prompt: A map labels every Lapita island as settled by 1200 BCE. Explain how you would check and revise it.
activity.response: Compare each island’s dated settlement evidence with the regional overview. Do not use the early Bismarck frame to backdate Tonga or every other island. Mark unverified or later local sequences separately.

snapshots.text: Around 1200 BCE belongs within the broad Bismarck Lapita frame and near the later boundary of An Sơn’s selected burial sequence. Remote Oceanian settlement and individual Tongan sites require their own later or overlapping dates. This snapshot does not establish one contemporaneous chain of settled islands.

citations.locator: Bismarck emergence and Remote Oceania 1100–800 BCE

title: Ceremonial places and the histories of particular objects
question: How do we connect a portable image to a place without inventing its findspot?

summary.title: Chavín and Gulf Coast centres
summary.text: Chavín’s galleries, plazas and carved imagery offer one Andean ceremonial setting. San Lorenzo and La Venta offer distinct Gulf Coast histories of earth building and offerings. Comparing them asks how objects and built spaces shaped collective activity, without proposing one American religion or a connection demonstrated by resemblance alone.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: galleries, plazas and imagery

sections.title: An object travels with a different record
sections.text: The selected Chavín-style textile is a museum object with its own attribution and date. It is not automatically an excavated furnishing from the highland ceremonial centre. Likewise, a regional ceramic attribution does not place the selected Olmec figure in a known San Lorenzo household. Object catalogues and site histories must be linked with evidence, not just a shared label.

sections.title: A coastal setting at the later date
sections.text: For around 300 BCE, the Met’s Andean chronology describes Paracas Peninsula burials wrapped in layers of cloth and embroidered textiles. This is a coastal funerary setting with its own evidence. It supplies a dated comparison without extending the Chavín centre’s disputed endpoint or assigning the selected museum textile to a Paracas burial.

citations.locator: Key Events c300 BCE: funerary bundles

sections.title: Different endpoints change a snapshot
sections.text: UNESCO’s Chavín Description uses 1500–300 BCE, while its Brief synthesis gives the fifteenth through fifth centuries BCE. The discrepancy remains visible. The Gulf Coast account describes changes in prominent centres and continuing production elsewhere. Neither account supports the disappearance of every community at a single boundary.

perspectives: Ceremonial architecture and collected objects favour durable, selected remains. The people who made textiles, carried materials or maintained spaces are not represented by a complete set of personal accounts.
scope: Two named regional settings, with later Colima as a separate reading destination. The Chavín date conflict is unresolved; a broad cultural label cannot settle the chronology of every building.

activity.prompt: A caption places the museum textile inside Chavín’s temple in 300 BCE. Identify the two independent evidence checks that caption needs.
activity.response: Check excavation provenance before assigning the textile to the temple, and check its own date against the site’s conflicting chronology. Stylistic similarity alone supplies neither a findspot nor a precise year.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE, the museum chronology describes textile-wrapped burials on the Paracas Peninsula. This coastal setting supplies a dated comparison. Chavín’s conflicting summary endpoints remain unresolved; the selected museum textile is not assigned to a Paracas burial, and the later Colima case is not backdated.

citations.locator: Key Events c300 BCE: funerary bundles

title: Kushite institutions from Kawa to the Meroe region
question: How can temples, workshops and burial places reveal changes in royal organization?

summary.title: Several centres, separate histories
summary.text: Taharqo’s temple projects at Kawa and Sanam belong to an earlier Kushite royal setting. Meroe, Naqa and Musawwarat es-Sufra provide a broader view of urban, religious and productive spaces. Their remains span many centuries and should not be collapsed into one ruler’s reign.

sections.title: Royal claims and working materials
sections.text: Kawa’s inscriptions claim arrangements for craftspeople and construction. Those are royal statements about work, not the workers’ own testimony. The later Meroe-region evidence includes production and water installations as well as temples and tombs, widening the questions beyond the image of a king alone.

sections.title: A change of burial centre is not a single population move
sections.text: UNESCO places most royal burials at Meroe from the third century BCE onward. That transition comes long after Taharqo’s reign. It helps orient a change in royal practice, but does not date every monument or imply that all households moved at once.

perspectives: Monuments and royal inscriptions foreground rulers. Workshops and water systems make other work visible, while leaving individual obligations and experiences incompletely recorded.
scope: Selected Nile and Kushite centres. No claim that all surviving Meroe-region monuments already existed in 300 BCE; the earlier shabti retains its own date and probable provenance.

activity.prompt: Explain why a royal inscription and an excavated workshop might support different statements about a building project.
activity.response: An inscription records what a ruler claimed to organize. Workshop remains support particular production activities. Use both while keeping the royal voice, archaeological interpretation and missing workers’ testimony distinct.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE marks the approach to the third-century BCE shift toward most royal burials at Meroe in UNESCO’s account. It is a broad transition marker, not an exact relocation event. Taharqo’s seventh-century BCE objects are earlier comparisons.

title: Public work and power in changing Greek settings
question: Is using public space the same as having a share in government?

summary.title: Athens and the later Hellenistic world
summary.text: Athenian water carrying brings household work into public space. Formal civic participation followed narrower rules. Later Hellenistic kingdoms and alliances place those questions within changing political settings, rather than extending one version of Athenian democracy across all Greek communities.

sections.title: Necessary work and political eligibility differ
sections.text: The hydria’s fountain scene can prompt questions about obtaining water. Literary and archaeological interpretation includes both free and enslaved women in public activity. The constitutional account’s male civic enrollment rules answer a different question: who could qualify for particular political roles.

sections.title: Patronage shifts with political settings
sections.text: After Alexander’s death in 323 BCE, successor rulers and Greek alliances shaped a different political landscape. Royal commissions supported buildings, sculpture and luxury production. Later, Rome became another centre employing Greek artists. These changes in patrons do not establish an identical experience for every craft worker.

citations.locator: Opening chronology; patronage; first-century BCE Rome

perspectives: The evidence separates people doing essential work from the narrower categories represented in political institutions. Images and official descriptions do not recover every excluded person’s experience.
scope: Athens is the close local inquiry; Hellenistic kingdoms and later Rome are dated comparisons. The sixth-century BCE jar is not a direct view of public life in 300 BCE.

activity.prompt: Give one reason a person might be visible at a public fountain but absent from a list of eligible political participants.
activity.response: Public work and residence do not by themselves establish the citizenship, status, age or gender eligibility described for particular institutions. A strong response distinguishes the image’s subject from the constitutional rule.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE falls after Alexander’s death and within the emerging Hellenistic political setting. Earlier Athenian objects and institutional descriptions offer comparisons, not proof that every Greek city retained the same arrangements at this date.

title: Royal centres and the work of governing across distance
question: How do buildings and images present power differently from administrative arrangements?

summary.title: Nimrud, Susa and Persepolis
summary.text: Nimrud’s palace reliefs present an Assyrian royal setting. Later Achaemenid building at Susa and Persepolis presents another imperial history. Their images help investigate how rulers represented power, while roads, governors and palace work raise practical questions about maintaining institutions.

citations.locator: Darius: roads, satraps and building projects

sections.title: An image of agreement is a claim
sections.text: At Persepolis, reliefs show people from different parts of the empire approaching or supporting the king. The arrangement presents imperial order. It cannot establish that every represented community agreed with the ruler or that obligations were experienced equally.

citations.locator: Persepolis reliefs and the impression of harmony

sections.title: Successor kingdoms need a new date frame
sections.text: Alexander’s conquest ended Achaemenid rule; after his death, successor kingdoms emerged, including the Seleucids in the Near East. The 300 BCE setting therefore cannot be represented simply by extending Ashurnasirpal II’s Nimrud or the Achaemenid court into the future.

perspectives: Royal monuments privilege the court’s desired image. Labour, tribute and administration involved people whose perspectives are only partly recoverable through those monuments.
scope: Selected royal centres and a successor-era orientation, not a complete West/Central Asian history. Similar palace imagery does not prove identical institutions or unbroken dynastic continuity.

activity.prompt: A relief depicts orderly tribute bearers. Write one observation and one claim that the relief cannot establish on its own.
activity.response: Observe the represented arrangement and figures. Do not treat the image as evidence of universal consent or equal obligations; those require other records and perspectives.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE belongs to the successor-kingdom setting after Alexander, including Seleucid power in the Near East. The Assyrian and Achaemenid palace readings are earlier institutional comparisons, not courts still ruling at this date.

title: Mauryan government before and during Ashoka
question: How does an official message differ from evidence that its instructions were followed?

summary.title: Pataliputra and audiences farther away
summary.text: Candragupta Maurya established rule from Pataliputra before Ashoka’s reign. Later inscriptions carried Ashoka’s policies to differently situated audiences, including Greek and Aramaic material at Kandahar. A capital, a message and its recipients are related but distinct parts of government.

citations.locator: Opening dynastic history; languages and inscriptions

sections.title: Messages needed language, materials and people
sections.text: Writing in different languages made official messages available in different settings. It did not mean that everyone could read them or that officials carried out every instruction. The linked edicts let readers inspect specific announced actions and compare royal ideals with the practical problem of implementation.

citations.locator: Girnar II, printed pp3–4; Dhauli Separate I, pp95–97

sections.title: Do not backdate the later ruler
sections.text: The university account places Candragupta’s transfer of power to Bindusara around 297–298 BCE and Ashoka’s reign around 268–232 BCE. The 300 BCE snapshot therefore precedes Ashoka’s inscriptions. Later evidence can illuminate a developing institution without becoming contemporary evidence for its earlier phase.

perspectives: Royal proclamations preserve the ruler’s chosen presentation. Recipients, officials and communities could have different experiences that the inscription itself does not settle.
scope: A justified institutional focus connecting a capital and differently addressed borderland messages. Not all South Asian communities were governed or addressed in the same way; later religious traditions remain distinct from contemporary inscriptions.

activity.prompt: An edict announces wells along roads. What is the difference between proving the announcement and proving its full implementation?
activity.response: The inscription supports that the ruler announced the policy. Dating and examining wells, administrative records and local evidence would be needed to assess where and how it was implemented.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE belongs to the early Mauryan setting under Candragupta, shortly before the source’s approximate transfer to Bindusara. Ashoka’s later inscriptions are a next reading, not evidence already issued at this snapshot date.

citations.locator: Opening paragraphs: succession c297–298 BCE; Ashoka c268–232 BCE

title: From competing states to imperial administration
question: What changes when rules and records must work across a larger territory?

summary.title: Qin, Chu and later imperial centres
summary.text: The Warring States frame includes competing polities rather than a single Qin empire. Chu’s lacquer and silk-painting evidence adds a distinct setting to the later Qin administrative inquiry. Court histories, craft objects and local records each expose different activities.

citations.locator: Timeline; 770 BCE and c400–200 BCE entries

sections.title: Common rules required practical handling
sections.text: The later Qin inquiry compares devices for measuring different quantities and wood documents used in county administration. The Liye records show that applying common requirements still involved choices about materials, layout and handling. A decree and its local paperwork need to be studied together.

sections.title: The empire follows the snapshot
sections.text: The museum’s Warring States convention runs from 475 to 221 BCE; imperial Qin follows in 221–206 BCE. Western Han then developed its capital at Chang’an. These changes do not make the later documents, tombs or capital features contemporary with 300 BCE.

perspectives: Administrative documents preserve tasks and categories useful to officials. Craft and material choices reveal other work, while leaving many workers’ own accounts unrecorded.
scope: Selected Chinese state and administrative settings, not all East Asia. The museum chronology’s inconsistent Qin Key Events heading is not adopted; its timeline and separate Qin essay establish the imperial dates.

activity.prompt: Explain why a later imperial measuring device cannot demonstrate that all states used one system in 300 BCE.
activity.response: Its date belongs to the later imperial frame. Establishing earlier uniformity would require contemporary evidence across the separate states, not a backward projection from an imperial decree.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE lies within the Warring States period, before imperial Qin. Chu and Qin provide distinct political settings; the later standardization and Liye paperwork are comparisons across a transition, not documents from this selected year.

title: Bronze deposits and changing island pottery traditions
question: Why does a change in objects not automatically mean the disappearance of a people?

summary.title: Vietnamese contexts and Tongan sequences
summary.text: Đông Sơn-associated drums occur in different kinds of deposits. Tonga’s earlier decorated pottery and later plainware provide a separate island history. Comparing them makes the relationship between an object category, a dated deposit and a community an explicit question.

sections.title: Find context changes the question
sections.text: A drum containing tools at Cổ Loa and a drum associated with a wooden container at Phú Chánh do not provide identical evidence of use. The small museum drum has another collection history. Their dates and contexts must be established independently before drawing conclusions about shared ritual or ordinary work.

sections.title: A ceramic endpoint is not a human endpoint
sections.text: The Tongan study argues that ceramic manufacture had ceased by about 400 BCE after a period of plainware production. That is a claim about a material practice. It does not establish the end of settlement or the disappearance of island communities, and it cannot be used as a uniform Pacific boundary.

perspectives: Objects preserve selected activities and deposits. Neither a museum classification nor the absence of later pottery gives a full account of how people identified themselves.
scope: Separate mainland and island comparisons, with no contact inferred between them. Later Phú Chánh and Luy Lâu evidence is not moved into the 300 BCE snapshot; it remains available in the dossier with its own dates.

activity.prompt: Rewrite “pottery stops, so the people vanished” using the evidence and one unanswered question.
activity.response: The study dates a change or end in ceramic manufacture. Ask what other settlement, food or material evidence could establish later community life; the pottery sequence alone cannot answer that question.

snapshots.text: Around 300 BCE falls within the broad Đông Sơn-associated frame. Individual drums and deposits still need their own dates. In Tonga it is later than the study’s proposed end of pottery manufacture; that material boundary does not demonstrate that island communities ended.

citations.locator: Abstract and Discussion: manufacture ceased by c400 BCE

title: Households and shared places across American communities
question: How did household work support larger gathering places?

summary.title: Teotihuacan, Ohio and Moche valleys
summary.text: Teotihuacan’s neighbourhoods, Ohio’s earthwork gathering places and Moche valley communities reveal different relationships between domestic work and shared institutions. Their surviving buildings and objects do not establish one political system or contact among all three settings.

sections.title: Monuments depended on everyday work
sections.text: Apartment compounds at Teotihuacan bring household activities into an urban history often dominated by monuments. At Mound City, construction and ceremonial gathering form another setting for collective effort. Moche household archaeology instead supplies local sequences of production and domestic space. Monument size alone does not reveal who assigned the work.

sections.title: Later buildings cannot fill an earlier moment
sections.text: These places changed over centuries. The full apartment history at Teotihuacan, a particular earthwork wall, and a later Moche household deposit are not all dated to 200 CE. The Bering Strait reading begins later still; it extends the chapter’s inquiry without supplying a northern case for this exact snapshot.

scope: Three selected settings, with later Bering evidence kept separate. Local building episodes and sampled deposits retain their own dates.
perspectives: Household and production remains make ordinary tasks visible without recovering each worker’s status or testimony.

activity.prompt: Compare an apartment compound and an earthwork enclosure. What would you need before claiming both used identical labour arrangements?
activity.response: Describe the distinct activities and local contexts. Seek evidence of recruitment, obligations and organization at each place; similar large projects do not establish identical institutions.

snapshots.text: Around 200 CE, Teotihuacan, Ohio gathering traditions and Moche valley communities provide distinct regional settings. The broad overlap permits comparison, not the assignment of every later apartment, mound or workshop to this year.

title: Aksum, Adulis and the Meroe region
question: How can inland work and exchange be read alongside royal monuments?

summary.title: Ports and inland centres
summary.text: Adulis was a coastal outlet connected with inland Aksum in an early merchant account. Farther northwest, Meroe and its associated centres preserve a different Nile-region history. These settings broaden the view beyond a single port or monumental capital.

citations.locator: Excerpt pp5–7: Adulis and inland connection

sections.title: Moving goods required work in particular places
sections.text: The merchant account describes exchange from a commercial perspective. Meroe-region remains include production and water installations alongside temples and burials. Such evidence makes provisioning and skilled work part of institutional history without supplying the route of every traded object.

sections.title: An excavated deposit has several dates
sections.text: Beta Samati’s later deposits combine objects with different manufacture dates. The investigators use coins, pottery and radiocarbon evidence together. These later inland findings are useful for following change, but cannot all be projected back to 200 CE or treated as one contemporary assemblage.

citations.locator: Printed pp1540–1543; Figure4 and upper-deposit chronology

scope: Separate Horn/Red Sea and Nile settings. The first-century account and later inland deposits are dated comparisons around a broad regional frame, not a census of Africa in 200 CE.
perspectives: Merchant and royal records favour particular interests. Food preparation and production debris expose additional work while leaving many individual voices absent.

activity.prompt: An old coin appears in a later deposit. Which dates must you distinguish before using it to date the whole site?
activity.response: Separate manufacture, circulation, deposition and excavation. Compare stratigraphy, pottery and independent dates before assigning the deposit or site a date.

snapshots.text: Around 200 CE falls within the selected Aksumite and Meroe-region histories. The early Adulis account offers preceding evidence of coastal–inland exchange; Beta Samati’s later finds are follow-through, not objects automatically deposited in this year.

title: Roman households, provincial power and later change
question: How did legal status and practical work differ across an empire?

summary.title: Rome and its provinces
summary.text: The Severan court connected people and places beyond Italy: Septimius Severus came from Leptis Magna, and Julia Domna from Syria. Governing involved armies and provincial institutions as well as a court. Rome was a centre of authority, not a model for every household under its rule.

sections.title: Occupation did not determine legal status
sections.text: Agriculture, craft and services supported towns and armies. The museum guide distinguishes occupations from the legal positions of enslaved, freed and freeborn people. Two people doing similar work could therefore have very different rights and opportunities.

sections.title: Institutions changed after the snapshot
sections.text: The grant of citizenship in 212 CE and the later development of Constantinople belong after 200 CE. The Middle Byzantine ivory in the linked reading is much later still. These are opportunities to compare changing institutions, not reasons to widen the Severan object’s date.

scope: A Roman imperial focus connecting Rome with provincial settings; later Constantinople is a dated comparison. It does not represent every European community.
perspectives: Elite portraits favour ruling families; work and legal categories help recover other positions without making everyone’s experience equivalent.

activity.prompt: Why does naming a person’s job not establish that person’s rights?
activity.response: Use the distinction between occupation and legal status. Work of the same kind could be performed by people with different status; a stronger claim needs evidence about the particular person.

snapshots.text: Around 200 CE belongs to Severan rule. Caracalla’s later citizenship grant in 212 CE has not yet occurred, and Constantinople’s later imperial history is not backdated. The portrait and household inquiry remain grounded in their own ranges.

title: Palmyra and Parthian centres: exchange within political settings
question: What can a trading city tell us beyond a line on a route map?

summary.title: Palmyra and Ctesiphon
summary.text: Palmyra’s family memorials and civic rules give a local view of transactions and public life. Ctesiphon was a principal Parthian royal residence farther east. Their histories invite comparison of civic and royal institutions without making Palmyra merely a stop on an invented itinerary.

sections.title: Exchange had rules and patrons
sections.text: Palmyra’s tax text records particular regulated transactions, rather than all trade everywhere. The Parthian account connects wealth and artistic patronage, while acknowledging that much art from the capitals is lost. Surviving edge-region objects cannot simply stand in for every missing capital context.

sections.title: A later political transition
sections.text: Parthian rule ended with the Sasanian takeover in the early third century CE. That change follows the 200 CE snapshot. Palmyra’s own later conflicts and continuing history must also retain separate dates, rather than become one universal regional collapse.

scope: Selected Syrian and Mesopotamian settings. No continuous caravan itinerary or uniform political history is inferred from objects or regional overlap.
perspectives: Family memorials and civic rules preserve different priorities from royal accounts. Traders, carriers and workers remain unevenly represented.

activity.prompt: Why is a tax rule evidence of a civic arrangement but not a complete record of every transaction?
activity.response: It states selected rules or categories. Establishing actual compliance and the full volume or routes of exchange requires other evidence.

snapshots.text: Around 200 CE, Palmyra’s civic setting coexists with the late Parthian world. The Sasanian takeover of 224 CE comes later. These dates locate distinct institutions; they do not supply a journey taken by every object.

title: Kushan images, temple orders and practical maintenance
question: How did a royal command become work at a particular sanctuary?

summary.title: Rabatak and Surkh Kotal
summary.text: The Rabatak inscription records royal and dynastic instructions concerning a temple. Surkh Kotal’s inscription concerns a water problem and building work. These named settings let us compare the announcement of authority with practical maintenance.

sections.title: Named intermediaries matter
sections.text: The Surkh Kotal account credits Nukunzuk with work on water provision; a version also names Burzmihr and the writer Mihraman. Such details shift attention from the ruler’s image to people involved in carrying out and recording a project. They remain statements in an inscription, not a complete workforce account.

citations.locator: Printed pp78–79: SK4 and version M

sections.title: The remembered event and the surviving record
sections.text: Sims-Williams separates Rabatak’s account of first-year orders from possible indications of a later inscription date. The selected coin has another catalogue date. Reading them together requires several clocks rather than one date for every expression of Kushan rule.

scope: A justified institutional focus across two sanctuaries in present-day Afghanistan and a separately catalogued coin. It does not cover all South Asia or resolve every debated Kanishka-era convention.
perspectives: Inscriptions name some officials and a writer but do not preserve every builder’s or worshipper’s account.

activity.prompt: How would you label an inscription that remembers an earlier command?
activity.response: State the command’s reported date separately from the proposed date of the surviving inscription. Keep the dating debate visible rather than making the record contemporary by assumption.

snapshots.text: Around 200 CE lies within the broad Kushan frame. The selected coin and sanctuary inscriptions refer to separately dated earlier events and records; they are evidence for an institutional history, not proof that those works occurred in this year.

title: Han capitals and the work represented in tomb models
question: How do models and policy proposals illuminate different parts of household production?

summary.title: Chang’an, Luoyang and represented estates
summary.text: The Han account distinguishes a western capital phase from the restored Eastern Han court. Tomb models of towers, granaries and wells introduce another scale: the resources and buildings associated with estates. These are representations made for funerary use, not measured plans of one surviving farm.

citations.locator: Western Han and Eastern Han paragraphs

sections.title: Storage and water supported repeated work
sections.text: A granary points toward keeping food available beyond harvest; a well toward access to water. Together with the tower, the models invite questions about provision and household standing. Their presence in a tomb does not recover exact crop yields, ownership arrangements or workers’ conditions.

sections.title: After Han, several political centres
sections.text: After 220 CE, the museum chronology distinguishes Wei, Wu and Shu, followed by Jin and later overlapping northern and southern regimes. These categories describe changing political arrangements, not the disappearance of farming or skilled work. Later political histories need their own evidence rather than an extension of the Eastern Han label.

sections.title: Earlier policy is not a later estate ledger
sections.text: Chao Cuo’s 178 BCE proposal connected grain deliveries with rank and penalties. It is much earlier than many Eastern Han models. The Han frame ends in 220 CE, after this chapter’s snapshot; neither the earlier proposal nor that later boundary dates every model or household.

scope: A focused Chinese imperial and household inquiry with distinct capitals and evidence types. It does not stand for every East Asian community or turn funerary objects into literal buildings.
perspectives: Models express selected expectations of provision and standing; policy prose foregrounds an adviser’s concerns. Farm workers’ own testimony is less visible.

activity.prompt: Compare the evidence supplied by a model granary and an adviser’s proposal about grain.
activity.response: The model represents a structure and expectations of provision; the proposal recommends an administrative action. Neither alone proves the actual yield or rules of a particular estate.

snapshots.text: Around 200 CE belongs to Eastern Han, before the conventional 220 CE endpoint. Broadly dated tomb models support a household-provisioning inquiry. Chao Cuo’s much earlier proposal remains a comparison, not a regulation documented for this year.

title: Mekong exchange, bronze working and Tongan settlement
question: How can a regional overview and an excavated workshop answer different questions?

summary.title: Óc Eo and northern Vietnamese contexts
summary.text: The national museum places Óc Eo in the lower Mekong and delta, within a broad first–seventh-century CE setting of exchange. Northern drum finds and later Luy Lâu production evidence belong to different places and dates. Their comparison should not turn them into one city or one political system.

sections.title: Exchange and production need different evidence
sections.text: The museum overview describes ports and interregional exchange. At Luy Lâu, moulds and production debris supply a more local question about how bronze objects were made. A regional trade description does not date each workshop or identify the route of a particular drum.

sections.title: Island settlement after pottery
sections.text: The Tongan study describes occupation continuing from ceramic into later aceramic periods at its sampled sites. Holopeka, Fakala’a and Moisa began in the plainware phase and continued later. This independently researched island sequence distinguishes settlement from pottery manufacture; it is not evidence for contact with the Mekong.

citations.locator: Methods: site continuity and three exceptions

sections.title: Displayed objects can be later than the opening frame
sections.text: The Óc Eo page lists coins and rings dated to the fifth–sixth centuries and a wooden Buddhist statue to the fifth–seventh. Those objects cannot illustrate 200 CE simply because the regional heading begins in the first century. Later workshop evidence must be handled with the same care.

citations.locator: Artifact captions: coins, rings, wooden statue

scope: Separate mainland and Tongan settings. The study describes settlement continuity into later aceramic periods, not a precisely dated 200 CE floor or evidence of contact with Vietnam. The Óc Eo overview does not establish exact borders or a first port.
perspectives: Museum overviews and archaeological finds expose different scales of work, but neither records all inhabitants’ experiences.

activity.prompt: Why should a fifth-century coin remain outside a display specifically labelled 200 CE?
activity.response: Its own catalogue date takes precedence over a broad regional heading. Use it as an explicitly later comparison, or find evidence independently dated to the selected moment.

snapshots.text: Around 200 CE falls within the museum’s broad lower-Mekong Óc Eo frame. Its displayed fifth–seventh-century objects and later Luy Lâu workshop finds are not backdated. Tongan research separately describes settlement continuing into later aceramic periods; it does not identify an exact event in this year.

title: Maya households and the beginnings of Chaco great houses
question: How can we compare work without making different communities contemporary by assumption?

summary.title: Courtly containers and village provision
summary.text: The selected Maya cup connects a named owner with food and imagery. Excavated Cerén households offer a different view: food production, part-time specialties and exchange. These settings bring makers and household provision into a history otherwise easily dominated by courtly objects.

sections.title: Building over generations
sections.text: Farther north, Pueblo Bonito was constructed in stages from about 850 to 1150 CE. Its rooms and masonry are the accumulated results of work over generations. A photograph of the whole structure therefore cannot show what stood at the beginning of construction.

sections.title: Objects and buildings keep different clocks
sections.text: The Maya cup’s seventh–eighth-century catalogue date precedes the 850 CE snapshot. The Chaco cacao study’s sampled vessels are later, around 1000–1125. Comparing their evidence is useful, but neither supplies a documented cacao-drinking event at Chaco in 850 or a route taken by this Maya vessel.

scope: A comparison of Maya court/village evidence and an Ancestral Puebloan building sequence. Neither is a summary of all American communities; the objects and deposits do not share one date.
perspectives: Courtly writing names an owner. Household archaeology and building remains reveal other tasks, while often leaving individual workers unnamed.

activity.prompt: Could a photograph of completed Pueblo Bonito illustrate the site as it looked in 850 CE?
activity.response: Use it to introduce the conserved site, with a clear caption. Reconstructing 850 requires evidence for the earliest building phases; the complete later footprint cannot be backdated.

snapshots.text: Around 850 CE marks the approximate beginning of Pueblo Bonito’s staged construction, not completion of the great house. The selected Maya cup is earlier; the sampled Chaco cacao vessels are later. Their comparison does not establish an exchange between those particular objects or communities in this year.

title: Middle Niger towns and earlier Aksumite work
question: Must a town begin with a palace or a foreign trading expedition?

summary.title: Djenné-Djeno and its neighbours
summary.text: Excavations and settlement survey place Djenné-Djeno’s growth within the first millennium CE, with a high point around 750–1100. Nearby settlements were part of this urban landscape. This history precedes the Mali Empire explored in the linked dossier; the later royal map cannot explain the origins of these towns.

sections.title: Food and materials connected settlements
sections.text: The excavation report considers rice, fish and other local products alongside imported stone and iron. Urban exchange depended on supplies from a wider landscape, not only conspicuous imported luxuries. Its account challenges the idea that Middle Niger towns arose solely as an effect of later trans-Saharan trade.

citations.locator: Extract: staples, imported materials and interpretation

sections.title: An earlier eastern comparison
sections.text: Beta Samati in the Aksumite highlands preserves food preparation and small-scale production in separately dated deposits. This provides an earlier comparison for urban work, not a second African town established as occupied in 850 by those deposits. The two regions should not be forced into one sequence of rise and decline.

sections.title: Different town, different surviving fabric
sections.text: The UNESCO property includes Djenné-Djeno and other archaeological sites alongside the fabric of present Djenné. Later Islamic architecture must remain separate from the earlier settlement evidence. Buildings visible today are not automatically a picture of the ninth century.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: component sites and later town

scope: A Middle Niger focus with an explicitly earlier Horn comparison. The 1981 excavation report is consulted through its published extract, not a new analysis of all underlying finds. No continent-wide political model is inferred.
perspectives: Household remains and regional survey broaden the account beyond rulers. They do not recover every resident’s voice or prove that social differences were absent.

activity.prompt: Which evidence would help distinguish a town supported by its hinterland from a story based only on imported treasures?
activity.response: Look for local food production, ordinary tools, settlement relationships and dated exchange evidence. Explain what imported material adds without treating it as the sole cause of urban life.

snapshots.text: Around 850 CE lies within the excavation report’s 750–1100 high point for Djenné-Djeno and nearby settlements. This supplies a Middle Niger urban setting before the later Mali Empire. Aksumite deposits and the architecture of present Djenné retain their separate chronologies.

title: Aachen and Constantinople: buildings, images and changing authority
question: How can a building preserve several different political and religious moments?

summary.title: Two court settings
summary.text: Aachen’s palace chapel formed part of Charlemagne’s residence. Constantinople combined imperial and church institutions with craft production. Comparing them draws attention to the ways built spaces and images helped present authority; it does not make their governments or communities identical.

sections.title: Working with material and inherited forms
sections.text: Aachen’s octagonal core, galleries and bronze fittings bring skilled construction into the story. In Constantinople, the linked dossier distinguishes ivory carving from the fitting and repair of excavated ships. A courtly building or luxury object required work, but does not alone disclose each worker’s status.

sections.title: Later additions change what a visitor sees
sections.text: Aachen’s chapel was subsequently enlarged, and its present dome mosaic dates to 1880–1881. At Constantinople, disputes over religious images preceded the restoration of icons in 843. The selected tenth-century ivory is later than that transition; its date cannot be moved back to illustrate the precise moment.

scope: Two selected court and religious settings, not all of Europe. Aachen’s source offers overlapping early construction formulations; neither supplies a day-by-day schedule. No claim of a uniform European revival is adopted.
perspectives: Royal patronage and surviving religious objects are prominent; shipbuilding and material work expose additional activities without documenting all households.

activity.prompt: Which parts of a present-day building can safely be used to describe an earlier century?
activity.response: Identify separately dated fabric, later additions and restoration. Keep uncertain features labelled; a building’s foundation date is not the date of every visible element.

snapshots.text: By 850 CE Aachen’s early ninth-century chapel had been built, while Constantinople stood shortly after the 843 restoration of icons. The present Aachen mosaic and the selected Byzantine ivory belong to later dates and do not illustrate this exact year.

title: Baghdad, Samarra and the work of Abbasid workshops

summary.title: Cities with separate histories

title: Nalanda and Paharpur: sustaining places of learning

summary.title: Two monastic settings

title: Chang’an, Gyeongju and Nara: connected but distinct settings

title: Cahokia and Chaco: communities through urban change

summary.title: Neighbourhoods and gathering places
summary.text: Cahokia’s neighbourhood archaeology and Chaco’s great houses offer different views of organized work. Large public structures depended on recurring activities in homes and working places. Their size alone does not establish identical government, labour recruitment or social rank.

sections.text: At Cahokia, unfinished copper and workshop evidence reveal steps in production. At Chaco, masonry and timber record construction over generations. These practical traces answer questions about materials and skill, while the identities and conditions of every worker remain unknown.

title: Karakorum and Baghdad: work under changing imperial power

title: Song, Mongol and Ming settings: production across political change
question: How do we distinguish a craft history from a dynasty’s dates?

summary.title: Northern and southern settings

perspectives: Official proposals and elite collected objects preserve selected perspectives. Market and production evidence help recover wider work without establishing universal access or prosperity.

activity.response: Retain the vessel’s own date and label it as later. Compare techniques or institutions with supported earlier evidence rather than using a dynasty’s general fame to override object chronology.

title: Andean makers and a Pacific encounter

sections.text: Indigenous Andean makers continued techniques and forms while producing new combinations of motifs and commissions for churches and private patrons. perspectives: Makers and Indigenous uses of imported material complicate elite and colonial narratives. The ship’s written record remains a mediated colonial perspective, supplemented by village archaeology.

activity.response: Describe the find context and any use traces first. Compare competing interpretations; origin establishes where it was made, not automatically how a later user understood it.

title: Benin and Kongo: makers, translation and power
