sections.title: A book was a collaborative object
sections.text: Painters, calligraphers, illuminators and binders performed distinct work. Translation made Sanskrit narratives available in Persian, while surviving records sometimes name contributors. A painting’s subject is not a record of a historical event, and a name attached to one manuscript cannot supply the maker of another.

sections.title: The court moved; the evidence has several dates
sections.text: Fatehpur Sikri’s main building programme preceded the move to Lahore in 1585 described by the museum. The selected manuscript page has its own catalogue range. A reign, a court residence, a translation project and a surviving copy therefore cannot share a single automatic date.

scope: A justified focus on court book production across named residences, with Gujarat as a commercial context. It does not establish an agrarian census, universal literacy or the experience of every South Asian community.
perspectives: Named contributors help reveal collaboration beside royal patronage. Sources remain strongest for elite commissions and weaker for most producers and readers outside the court.

activity.prompt: Why should a translated story, its illustrated copy and a ruler’s reign receive separate dates?
activity.response: Identify the event or process each date describes. Translation, copying and illustration can happen at different times, and a reign only supplies an outer political frame.

snapshots.text: Around 1600 CE falls near the end of Akbar’s reign of 1556–1605. The workshop history includes earlier work at Fatehpur Sikri and Lahore, but the selected page must retain its own catalogue range. Neither residence nor every illustrated book is dated simply by the reign.

title: Ming workshops and Momoyama Japan
question: How did objects express authority while their makers worked within different institutions?

summary.title: Separate production settings
summary.text: Ming ceramic production involved court orders as well as other buyers. In Japan, the Momoyama account connects decorated castles and objects with competing warlords and changing power. These were distinct settings, not one East Asian style or shared government.

sections.title: A design still needed material work
sections.text: The selected Ming jar combines decoration below and above the glaze. Shaping, firing and surface work required coordinated skill. Japanese castle decoration and furnishings expressed another relationship between patrons and makers; visual splendour alone does not tell us the worker’s freedom or income.

sections.title: War and exchange were not opposites
sections.text: The museum’s Momoyama account describes continuing connections with China and Korea alongside Hideyoshi’s destructive invasions of Korea. It is therefore misleading to tell the period only through imported goods or artistic achievement. Later Tokugawa and Qing settings belong to subsequent political phases, not an unchanging 1600 map.

citations.locator: Final paragraph: invasions and overseas contacts

scope: Selected Chinese and Japanese production/patronage settings. The museum’s art-period convention 1573–1615 does not define every political transition; no total-isolation claim or uniformly beneficial exchange is adopted.
perspectives: Court and elite collections favour commissioned objects. The account keeps destructive war visible and does not infer ordinary experience from luxury surfaces.

activity.prompt: Why should an account of artistic exchange also examine war and coercion?
activity.response: Ask how people, materials and techniques moved, and who bore the costs. A beautiful object does not establish voluntary movement or benefit for all participants.

snapshots.text: Around 1600 CE falls within Ming rule and the museum’s Momoyama art-period frame in Japan. The selected Ming object has its own date; later Qing and Tokugawa institutions should not be imported into the snapshot as though their full later arrangements already existed.

title: Banda and Manila: exchange, provision and coercion
question: When does a trading relationship become an attempt to control people and food?

summary.title: Two maritime settings
summary.text: Banda’s spice exchange connected island production with imported food. The Manila system linked Philippine and American settings through Pacific voyages. These networks involved different local communities and institutions; a map of moving goods cannot by itself explain their working conditions.

sections.title: The first visit was not the later conquest
sections.text: The Westfries Museum account dates the first Dutch visit to Banda to 1599, before the VOC existed. It describes purchases and port fees before later treaty claims and violence. Keeping that sequence visible prevents the events of 1621 from replacing the islands’ earlier social and commercial history.

citations.locator: Opening 1599 visit; 1602 alliance and later escalation

sections.title: Control over trade could become control over survival
sections.text: The archive explains why restricting exchange endangered Banda’s food supply. Its 1621 records concern removal, destruction and coercion. The Manila shipbuilding accounts separately describe burdens on Philippine communities. Neither should be turned into a neutral story of efficient global connection.

sections.title: A Pacific comparison needs its own record
sections.text: The 1595 San Agustín wreck in Coast Miwok territory supplies a particular Pacific encounter. It is not evidence of a Banda–California voyage or a history of all Oceanian islands. The two maritime inquiries remain separate even when they share questions about provisions and work.

scope: Banda and the Philippine–American Pacific system, with no invented continuous route between them. The reading does not claim coverage of every Oceanian society or backdate VOC conquest to 1600.
perspectives: Colonial records dominate the archive and are read for their perspective. Bandanese communities and Philippine workers appear through different, uneven records rather than as anonymous cargo-route endpoints.

activity.prompt: Why is it misleading to label a 1599 encounter as the 1621 conquest?
activity.response: Keep initial purchases, subsequent coercive claims and the later conquest separately dated. Explain change over time without assuming that the first encounter already contained every later institution.

snapshots.text: Around 1600 CE follows the first Dutch visit to Banda in 1599 and the San Agustín wreck in 1595. The VOC’s later creation and Banda conquest of 1621 have not yet occurred. This earlier exchange setting is independently described rather than produced by extending the 1621 case backward.

title: Freedom, schooling and political participation
question: What changes when people win a declaration, a court case or an election?

summary.title: Saint-Domingue and Haiti
summary.text: In Saint-Domingue, people who had been enslaved fought to shape the meaning of emancipation. The French abolition decree of 1794 and Haitian independence in 1804 answered different questions: one concerned slavery, the other sovereignty. Neither date alone tells us how people could earn a living or exercise power afterward.

sections.title: Who could enter a classroom?
sections.text: In California, Mexican American families challenged segregation by local school districts. In Texas, Heman Sweatt challenged exclusion from a public law school. The courts addressed different institutions and questions. Reading the decisions side by side reveals how families and individuals tested public commitments in particular places.

citations.locator: Orange County family action and Ninth Circuit

sections.title: Political participation has a history beyond a single vote
sections.text: Mexico’s presidential election in 2000 brought an opposition candidate to office. The education ministry’s account distinguishes that transfer from the disagreements that followed. A change in office is something we can date; proving that it improved every citizen’s political voice would require further evidence.

citations.locator: Alternancia en el poder: election and subsequent disagreements

sections.title: A document can show one moment of work
sections.text: The linked Hine and Ojibwe readings ask who made a record and who supplied its interpretation. A reform photograph and later community knowledge can reveal tasks and relationships, but neither gives the unnamed subject’s complete testimony. The date of a photograph does not date the beginning of a practice.

citations.locator: Photograph LC-DIG-nclc-01451 and caption card no. 358

scope: Selected Caribbean, United States and Mexican settings. The legal examples are historical and differ in jurisdiction; no ruling or election is treated as continent-wide change.
perspectives: Formerly enslaved people, families bringing cases and voters appear as actors. Courts and governments record decisions more directly than the daily experience of everyone affected.

activity.prompt: Choose one victory in this reading. What did it change directly, and what would you need to know about its effects?
activity.response: Name the decision, year and jurisdiction. Then identify a different source—for example school enrolment, household testimony or later records—that could test implementation.

snapshots.text: In 1800, Saint-Domingue was still in the revolutionary struggle. The 1794 abolition decree preceded this moment; Haitian independence in 1804 had not yet been declared. Legal status, military control and the work of plantation communities cannot be reduced to a single date.

Around 1900, the 1896 Plessy decision remained a legal reference for enforced racial separation in the United States. Brown’s rejection of separate public schooling came in 1954. The intervening history must not be presented as though desegregation was already secured in 1900.

citations.locator: Historical introduction and opinion on Plessy

snapshots.text: In 1947 the Ninth Circuit upheld the ruling won by Mexican American families challenging segregation in Orange County schools. Mendez was a federal appeals decision, not the later US Supreme Court ruling in Brown and not a ruling integrating every school in the Americas.

In June 1950, the US Supreme Court ruled that Texas must admit Heman Sweatt to the University of Texas law school. It considered educational opportunities that could not be reduced to building size or a count of books. Brown’s broader public-school ruling was still four years away.

Mexico’s 2000 presidential election brought Vicente Fox, an opposition candidate, to office. This change after decades of rule by the dominant party is a specific political event. It does not establish that access to power or public services became equal for every citizen.

citations.locator: Election of Vicente Fox and limits of change

title: Asante and Benin courts, Gold Coast organizing and South African rights
question: What can an object, a political organization and a constitution each tell us about power?

summary.title: Skilled production and control
summary.text: At Kumasi, artisans made gold objects that expressed Asante court authority; gold also moved through tribute and war. Benin City was the centre of a different court. Britain’s 1897 attack and the later sale of looted works altered where objects could be seen and who could tell their histories.

citations.locator: Gold, tribute, artisans and court regulation

sections.title: Independence took organizing
sections.text: The United Gold Coast Convention formed in 1947. Nkrumah broke with it in 1949 and the Convention People’s Party launched its Positive Action campaign in 1950. An independence stamp of 1957 announced a later change, but the political work that preceded it included disagreement, strikes and repression.

citations.locator: Table A; Historical Setting: UGCC and Positive Action

sections.title: South Africa: voting and the limits of a promise
sections.text: The South African transition distinguished voting in 1994, constitutional signing in 1996 and commencement in 1997. The resulting text named rights and institutions; it did not measure whether every household could use those rights. A later national symbol similarly expresses an aspiration rather than proving an outcome.

scope: Asante/Gold Coast, Benin City and South Africa are distinct settings. The history of a particular museum acquisition is not the provenance of every Benin object.
perspectives: Court makers, organizers and voters broaden a story often told through rulers. Museum and government records still privilege particular institutions; a public emblem is not everyone’s testimony.

activity.prompt: How would you label a court object now in a museum if you know the general history of looting but not this object’s chain of custody?
activity.response: Give its supported production context, distinguish the documented attack from this object’s specific provenance, and say exactly which ownership steps remain unknown.

snapshots.text: Around 1800, Asante court production and gold exchange centred on institutions at Kumasi. The museum’s eighteenth–nineteenth-century weights and ornaments support this setting, without fixing their manufacture to 1800. These objects precede both the later Gold Coast colony and independent Ghana.

citations.locator: Court regulation and eighteenth–nineteenth-century object dates

snapshots.text: In 1900, British control was contested in Asante. In a separate setting, National Museums Scotland records purchases from a dealer during 1897–1903 following the British looting of Benin City. The two timelines concern different societies; the documented sales do not identify every object’s route.

In the Gold Coast in 1947, the United Gold Coast Convention formed. This was organization under colonial government, before the 1948 crisis, the later CPP split and 1957 independence. It supplies a specific African political setting without backdating the independence stamp.

In early 1950 the CPP’s Positive Action campaign called for strikes and resistance in the Gold Coast; leaders were imprisoned. The 1951 election and independence in 1957 came later. Political organizing did not mean that colonial executive power had already ended.

citations.locator: Historical Setting: Positive Action and 1951 election

snapshots.text: In April 2000 South Africa introduced a new coat of arms, after its first democratic election and the commencement of its final constitution. A new emblem marks a change in how the state presented itself; it cannot establish that unequal conditions had ended.

citations.locator: 2000: coat of arms on Freedom Day; constitutional milestones

title: Factory work, postwar recovery and institutions shared across borders
question: How can a proposal, an enacted rule and its effects have different dates?

summary.title: A mill needed rules and people to enforce them
summary.text: British cotton mills used apprentice labour around 1800. The 1802 legislation addressed apprentices; the 1833 Factory Act and its inspection system belong to a later stage. Surviving reports let us ask whether owners complied and what inspectors could actually see.

sections.title: After war, proposals became institutions in stages
sections.text: In 1947 George Marshall proposed American support for European recovery. The US law came in 1948. In 1950 Robert Schuman proposed sharing coal and steel production, especially between France and Germany. Reconstruction and political cooperation were related aims, but the speeches describe proposals, not instantaneous improvements in every home.

sections.title: A currency can change before the cash in a pocket
sections.text: The euro began in participating countries in 1999 for accounting and electronic payments. Euro notes and coins came in 2002. The distinction matters if a family story says what someone used to pay cash in 2000; a later coin cannot document that transaction.

scope: British industrial, French/German and selected participating European settings. These institutional changes did not encompass every European country or erase the uneven losses and displacement of war.
perspectives: Workers and households often appear indirectly in regulations, recovery proposals and monetary records. Their experiences require inspection reports, testimony and local evidence alongside the institutional dates.

activity.prompt: A museum label says a family paid cash with euro coins in France in 2000. How would you check it?
activity.response: Separate the 1999 currency launch from the 2002 issue of notes and coins. Ask whether the evidence describes accounting, electronic payment or physical cash, and identify the country.

snapshots.text: In Britain around 1800, apprentices worked in cotton mills before the 1802 apprentice legislation. The 1833 inspection system was still decades away. The later report in the factory dossier cannot be used as an inspector’s observation from 1800.

By 1900 Britain had already extended factory regulation beyond the earlier cotton-mill measures. Parliament’s 1867 extension is one dated step. A rule’s existence does not prove compliance in every workplace, and the earlier 1836 inspection material remains evidence from its own year.

On 5 June 1947 Marshall proposed a European plan for economic reconstruction with American assistance. Truman sent a related message to Congress in December. The legislation was signed in April 1948; a 1947 snapshot should show the proposal and need for recovery, not benefits already delivered under that Act.

citations.locator: 5 June speech, December message and 3 April 1948 Act

snapshots.text: On 9 May 1950 Schuman proposed placing French and German coal and steel production under common authority, open to other European participants. This is a dated proposal about resources, industry and war prevention, not evidence that every European state had already joined one organization.

citations.locator: Opening account and declaration: common High Authority

snapshots.text: In 2000 the euro existed for accounting and electronic payments in participating countries including France and Germany. National cash was still in use: euro banknotes and coins were introduced on 1 January 2002. Several European countries did not share the same currency timetable.

title: Qajar Iran, republican Türkiye and independent Kazakhstan
question: How can a photograph, a parliamentary record and a banknote establish different changes?

summary.title: Photographs at the Qajar court
summary.text: Qajar rulers governed Iran during the period conventionally dated 1785–1925. Photography arrived in the early 1840s and became one way the court presented itself and documented places. A staged image shows choices about representation; it cannot stand for all Iranian households.

citations.locator: Exhibition account: period, arrival of cameras and court missions

sections.title: The Ottoman imperial and republican settings differ
sections.text: After the First World War, an assembly met in Ankara in 1920 and proclaimed a republic in 1923. Parliamentary and electoral records describe formal changes in government. An American president’s 1947 request for assistance to Turkey and Greece reflects another government’s aims, not a survey of what Turkish citizens wanted.

citations.locator: New Parliament and Proclamation of the Republic

sections.title: In Central Asia, sovereignty also had practical forms
sections.text: Kazakhstan’s independence in 1991 and the introduction of the tenge in 1993 were separate steps. A banknote factory opened in 1995. Currency therefore offers a way to investigate the work of building institutions after Soviet rule, alongside the earlier Soviet space programme in the linked dossier.

scope: A Qajar court, selected Turkish institutions and Kazakhstan provide three local histories; neither an imperial label nor a modern border defines the whole region across two centuries.
perspectives: Court photographs, assemblies and a central bank speak from institutional positions. They document acts and objects more readily than regional differences, opposition voices or household purchasing power.

activity.prompt: Which would best date a political declaration, the creation of a currency and a family’s change in buying power?
activity.response: Use the declaration for the legal act and currency records for issue dates. Household income, prices and testimony would be needed for buying power; neither a new note nor a declaration alone establishes it.

snapshots.text: Around 1800 Iran was under Qajar rule, after the earlier Zand setting. The court photography discussed in this reading began only after cameras arrived in the 1840s. A Qajar photograph must not be backdated simply because the dynasty already existed.

In 1900 Qajar rule continued in Iran. The Berlin exhibition identifies a court photograph from 1893 and explains how photography helped construct images of rule. It supplies nearby dated evidence, not a picture taken in 1900 or an unfiltered view of all society.

In March 1947 Truman asked the US Congress for military and economic assistance to Greece and Turkey. Turkey’s republic had been proclaimed in 1923. The message records an American policy request, not money already received by every intended recipient or unanimous Turkish support.

Türkiye’s parliamentary election table records a general election on 14 May 1950. That entry establishes a dated electoral process; it does not by itself explain every voter’s choice or the extent of participation in each community. The selected Sputnik launch of 1957 still lay ahead.

By 2000 Kazakhstan had declared independence and introduced its own currency. The national bank dates those events to 1991 and 1993 respectively, and its banknote factory to 1995. These steps connect sovereignty with production without equating a change of currency with a guaranteed rise in living standards.

title: Company rule, Partition and the making of new political maps
question: When does changing a boundary also change the choices available to a household?

summary.title: Company territory was made through power
summary.text: Around 1800 the East India Company held territory under parliamentary oversight. Conquest and alliances expanded its holdings unevenly. In 1858 the British Crown took over the Company’s Indian possessions and armed forces; neither map nor administrative responsibility stayed fixed.

sections.title: A new border could divide a home from familiar places
sections.text: In 1947 independence and Partition divided Punjab and Bengal. A boundary map and official correspondence describe political decisions; later testimony can reveal uncertainty, displacement and loss that are harder to see on a map. Neither makes one household’s experience universal.

sections.title: New constitutions and internal boundaries came later
sections.text: India’s Constitution distinguished provisions effective immediately from general commencement in 1950. In 2000 Jharkhand became a state within India through the reorganization of Bihar. An internal state boundary and the 1947 international partition are different changes, even when both appear as lines on a map.

scope: Selected British Indian, Punjab/Bengal and post-independence Indian settings. The Indian commencement date is not a constitutional date for Pakistan or every South Asian state; internal reorganization is not another international partition.
perspectives: Official maps and laws are strong evidence of formal decisions. Compare them with personal records when asking about displacement, safety, language, work or the ability to return home.

activity.prompt: How would you distinguish a change of sovereign state from a change of state boundary within a country?
activity.response: Name the level of government and the legal event first. Then ask whose residence, citizenship or administration changed, using household-level evidence before making claims about lived effects.

snapshots.text: Around 1800, the East India Company expanded holdings through conquest and alliance under Governor-General Wellesley. This was Company government subject to parliamentary oversight, not yet the Crown takeover of 1858 and not a single uniform control over the whole subcontinent.

By 1900 the Crown had taken over the East India Company’s Indian possessions and armed forces under the 1858 Act. The earlier Company administration should not be left unchanged on a 1900 map. Nor should the 1947 border be projected backward into this period.

In August 1947 British India was partitioned as India and Pakistan became independent. Punjab and Bengal were divided. The decisions were dated; people’s journeys, losses and efforts to find relatives extended beyond the month in which sovereignty changed.

citations.locator: Independence and Partition background; selected telegrams

snapshots.text: 26 January 1950 was the general commencement date of India’s Constitution. Article 394 expressly distinguishes provisions that came into force at once. Independence in 1947 and constitutional commencement in 1950 belong to separate moments, not a shared date for all South Asian governments.

On 15 November 2000 Jharkhand became a state within India, formed from districts of Bihar. This was an internal reorganization rather than independence from India. The official formation date establishes the boundary change, not its effects on every resident.

title: From imperial and industrial settings to constitutions, war and talks
question: Which records tell us that an institution changed, and which describe its effects?

summary.title: China and Japan were not on one timetable
summary.text: The Qing court governed China across both the 1800 and 1900 snapshots. In Japan, Tomioka’s silk mill belonged to a nineteenth-century industrial project. Imported technology had to be adapted and workers had to learn new tasks; calling it modernization does not explain how work felt to each person.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: opening and integrated production

sections.title: Postwar Japan: commencement required further work
sections.text: Japan’s new constitution came into force in May 1947. Other laws were revised and a new Diet convened. A constitutional date matters, but it is not the same thing as the completion of every change in public institutions or family life.

citations.locator: Enactment and first session of the Diet

sections.title: Korea: a resolution and a declaration answer different questions
sections.text: The UN Security Council’s June 1950 resolution called for hostilities to cease and for North Korean forces to withdraw. Fifty years later, leaders met in Pyongyang and issued a joint declaration. A record of a demand or an agreement establishes what was asked or agreed, not that fighting instantly ended or political division vanished.

scope: Chinese imperial, Japanese industrial and constitutional, and Korean conflict/diplomatic settings. These national and international records do not describe a single East Asian political trajectory.
perspectives: Workers, families and those affected by war are unevenly visible in collections made by governments and international institutions. A leader’s statement does not establish every resident’s view.

activity.prompt: Which source could prove that leaders agreed to talks, and what would you need before claiming that families were reunited?
activity.response: Use the declaration for the commitment. Look for separately dated implementation records and family accounts before describing actual reunions or their reach.

snapshots.text: Around 1800 in China the Qing dynasty was in power. The National Library of Australia’s account places this in the longer 1644–1911 period. The selected Japanese mill at Tomioka is a later nineteenth-century setting; its machinery cannot be used to show industry in 1800.

Around 1900 Qing rule still continued in China, while Japan’s Tomioka mill had already opened in 1872. The two dates compare an imperial framework with an institution for silk production. The opening date does not establish which employee, machine or workplace rule applied in 1900.

Japan’s Constitution took effect on 3 May 1947, following April elections and before the first Diet session under it later in May. The National Diet Library lists further legal changes needed for the new institutions. Commencement therefore has a precise date without implying instantaneous implementation.

On 25 June 1950 the UN Security Council adopted resolution 82 in response to the armed attack on the Republic of Korea, calling for a halt to hostilities and withdrawal of North Korean forces. This records an institutional response to war, not a ceasefire already carried out.

citations.locator: Action note 25 June 1950; resolution title and operative demands

snapshots.text: In June 2000 the leaders of North and South Korea met in Pyongyang. Their joint declaration included commitments concerning separated families and cooperation. A summit and a written commitment are verifiable; the declaration alone does not prove reunification or that every family gained contact.

citations.locator: Opening and clauses 3–4 of the joint declaration

title: Aotearoa, Western Samoa and Indonesia: different paths through colonial rule
question: Why do contact, signing, recognition and independence need separate dates?

summary.title: Aotearoa before and after 1840
summary.text: Sealers and whalers arriving from the 1790s brought new maritime encounters to Māori communities before Te Tiriti was signed. In 1840 rangatira considered promises and signed or declined in particular circumstances. The several texts and later Crown actions must be distinguished from an assumption of universal agreement.

citations.locator: Sealers and whalers:1791–2 and early trade

sections.title: Indonesia: proclamation did not end the war
sections.text: The 1945 proclamation in Jakarta was followed by fighting and negotiations. Dutch military operations in 1947, the 1949 transfer to a federal state and the 1950 unitary change are separate events. They did not settle every territorial dispute or define one common civilian experience.

sections.title: Western Samoa had its own political movement
sections.text: Western Samoa passed from German to New Zealand administration. The Mau opposed colonial rule; New Zealand Parliament’s account describes the violent repression of a 1929 protest. The 1961 legislation and independence effective on 1 January 1962 belong to a different chronology from both Indonesia and Aotearoa.

citations.locator: Administration, Mau, Western Samoa Act and commencement

scope: Three selected settings. Western Samoa’s dates do not apply to American Samoa; Indonesian sovereignty and later East Timorese self-determination are separate processes. No general Pacific independence date is inferred.
perspectives: Treaty texts, colonial military accounts and legislatures document institutional acts. Rangatira, Samoan organizers and Indonesian civilians had distinct experiences that official records only partly preserve.

activity.prompt: Make a label for the 1950 Indonesian change and another for Western Samoa in 1962. Why should they use different verbs?
activity.response: In 1950 Indonesia replaced a federal arrangement with a unitary state following earlier proclamation and transfer. Western Samoa became independent in 1962. Name the prior status and authority each act changed.

snapshots.text: Around 1800 sealers and whalers were reaching Aotearoa waters; the ministry dates early arrivals to 1791–2 and describes links with the Australian port at Sydney. Te Tiriti’s 1840 signing was still in the future. Maritime contact is not a declaration of sovereignty.

By 1900 women in New Zealand had obtained the parliamentary vote under the 1893 Electoral Act, after petition campaigns. That change concerned voting rights; it did not resolve disagreements over Māori authority or mean that every political office became open at the same moment.

The Dutch launched a major military operation in Indonesia in July 1947, nearly two years after the independence proclamation. The 1949 federal settlement and 1950 unitary state were still in the future. A proclamation, control of territory and international recognition are different historical claims.

In 1950 Indonesia ended the federal structure created by the 1949 settlement and became a unitary state. Western Samoa remained under New Zealand administration; its independence would take effect in 1962. The two settings cannot share one decolonization date.

In 2000 East Timor was under the UN transitional administration established in 1999, following the popular consultation. Independent Timor-Leste dates to May 2002. The 2000 transition was neither the Indonesian revolution of 1945–50 nor independence already achieved.

citations.locator: UNTAET:1999–2002, February 2000 and independence in May 2002
